m04_1.what: The knob sits on the side of the cylinder, so it faces 90° away from the front lens face. Yet both are drawn almost facing the camera: the knob is a nearly round, front-on disc, just like the front rim. Its axle is the yoke's pivot, so it should point along the line between the two yoke arms. That puts it close to the picture plane, and the knob should show as a narrow ellipse seen almost edge-on, not a round disc. The knob therefore disagrees with both the body and the yoke.

m04_2.what: The three lens circles are drawn as flatter, more tilted ellipses than the front rim around them. The rim reads as nearly face-on, but the lenses read as if seen at a steeper angle, so the lenses and the rim don't agree on how the front face is turned.

Both ends of the two truss tubes show round end-caps facing the viewer. The right ends show clear circular caps, and the left ends are also drawn capped and rounded. A straight tube seen from one viewpoint can show only one of its end faces, so at least one pair of ends contradicts the camera.

m05_1.what: There is no equals (=) key. The four operator keys are there, but no key can finish a calculation and show the result, so the calculator cannot fully do its job. The bottom-right spot, where = usually sits, is taken by an oversized + key. Leaving out minor keys (C, %, memory) would be a fair simplification, but = is the one key a basic calculator cannot work without.

The body is drawn tilted away and turned, with thick side walls showing and a steeply slanted bottom edge. Yet every key is drawn front-on with no foreshortening. The keys don't shrink, tilt or bunch toward the far side, and the far top-right keys (9, ÷) are about the same size as the near ones. The key rows and columns don't run parallel to the face's edges, so the keypad looks pasted flat onto the tilted body. This is the same fault as reviewer example 1.

The top edge is almost level while the bottom edge slants down steeply to the right. The edges of the rectangular face should meet at one vanishing point or stay parallel, but they don't agree. The face looks like a skewed trapezoid rather than a rectangle in perspective.
Both are drawn as level, front-facing rectangles, as if seen straight on. The surrounding body is seen at an angle, so they don't follow the tilt of the face they sit in.

m05_2.what: The calculator has no equals (=) key. It has digits, a decimal point and four operators, but no key to get a result, so it cannot finish a calculation. Every real basic calculator has one. Leaving it out is a missing functional part, not a simplification. The enlarged + key sits where = usually goes.

The body is turned away from the viewer: its left edge leans strongly and its bottom edge drops steeply to the right. Yet the keys are drawn almost front-on, as nearly square rectangles of the same size. Their rows run close to horizontal instead of parallel to the body's bottom edge, and their columns lean much less than the body's left edge. The keys don't shrink, tilt or bunch toward the far side, so the keypad reads like a flat sticker that doesn't sit on the tilted face. This is the same fault as the first example.

The grey display and the red solar strip are near-perfect front-facing rectangles with level top and bottom edges. They don't follow the slanted face around them, so the top of the face disagrees with how the body is drawn.

m16_2.what: The frame does not add up. The only scissor mechanism is one X across the front. Its upper ends end at the seat's front clips, and the armrest posts start at the same clips. The back legs are straight rigid posts with no cross-bracing on the sides or back. In a real folding chair the legs make an X on each side, or front and back, joined by hinged seat rails. This frame has no joints that would let it fold. It also has nothing on the sides to stop it racking sideways, so it could neither fold nor stand firmly.

Three tubes join at one fabric clip with no hinge or tube joint. The X-leg ends at the clip, and the armrest post rises from the same point at a different angle. Fabric clips cannot carry leg or armrest loads.
The back right leg and foot are not clearly shown. Only three feet can be read for certain, so it is unclear what holds up the back right corner.

The back-right leg and its foot are missing. The front feet and the back-left foot set up a footprint, and the fourth foot should sit up and to the left of the front-right foot, around the space just above the X hub. That space shows only open floor, so the chair stands on three visible feet and the footprint does not close.

m35_1.what: The grid does not seem to be 8×8. The board reads as roughly 6 rows by 8 columns, and the squares look stretched into rectangles, so it could not hold a real chess game. Everything else in the set stands and works.

The tabletop is seen from well above, with a deep top face, yet the plinth steps at grass level show only thin slivers of top face, as if seen almost level. With a raised camera, surfaces lower down should show at least as much top face as the tabletop, not less. So the bottom of the table looks like it was drawn from a lower viewpoint than the top.

The ellipses at the foot of each stool are as flat as the seat tops, or flatter. They sit farther below eye level, so they should be slightly rounder. This makes the stool bases look seen from eye level while the seats are seen from above, and the feet look a little less firmly planted on the ground plane.

m35_2.what: The tabletop is seen square-on: it is symmetric and shows no side face. The pedestal directly under it is turned about 30° to the camera and shows a broad front face plus a clearly lit right side face, on the collar, shaft and plinth alike. On a solid table the pedestal's faces should line up with the slab's edges, so the top and its support look as if they come from two different viewpoints.

The plinth is the lowest flat surface in the scene, so it should show the most open top face. Instead its top ledge is drawn as an almost edge-on sliver. Meanwhile the higher slab and the stool tops are both seen clearly from above. The plinth reads as seen from eye level, which disagrees with the high camera used everywhere else.

m36_1.what: The rope is three closed rings stacked around the post with no free end, knot or tie-off. A real rope wound around a bollard has ends, so this is rings, not a wrapped rope.

The posts stand next to the deck instead of carrying it. No crossbeam, bolt or notch joins any post to the deck or its beam. The deck is held up only by short stub legs, so the posts are decorative and do no structural work. The front-right post overlaps the deck edge without visibly joining it.

Each plank sits on its own row, shifted right of the one before it, and shows a thick front edge, like the risers of a staircase. The deck reads as stepping up toward the back rather than as one flat surface seen from above. The plank rows do not lie on one plane that follows the pier's side edges.

The front plank and the beam under it run perfectly level. The bases of the two front posts that hold them are at different heights: the right post meets the water clearly lower and nearer than the left post meets the sand. Either the front edge should slope down to the right to match the diagonal pier, or the posts should stand at the same depth. As drawn, the deck's front and its supports come from different views.

The two long sides of the pier stay almost parallel as they go back, while the planks get shorter and closer together with distance. The side edges should meet toward one vanishing point to match how much the planks foreshorten.

The back posts sit almost at eye level (the horizon), yet their tops are drawn as fairly open ovals, nearly as round as the tops of the front posts that are well below eye level. They should flatten into thin ellipses.

m36_2.what: The front edge is not one straight line. The left part (the board with bolts) sits higher, and the right end block sits lower and further forward. Its top and bottom edges do not continue the board's lines, so the deck's front corner looks broken or offset instead of being one square edge that recedes to the same point as the planks.

m04_1.what: The lamp below is seen from underneath at a three-quarter angle, but the truss is a flat, front-on ladder. None of its underside or depth shows, and the tubes have no foreshortening. The rails slope upward to the right and spread slightly apart there, yet the clamp block that grips them is square to the frame and front-on, so it does not turn with the rails.

The front rim is drawn almost as a full circle and the three LEDs as perfect front-on circles. At the same time, a long stretch of the cylinder's side and top is visible, which means the body is turned well away from the camera. With that much body showing, the rim ellipse and the LEDs should be noticeably narrower and foreshortened in the same direction.

m04_2.what: The two pivots don't sit on one cross-section of the cylinder. The left hub is at the front rim, ahead of the orange band, while the right hub is well behind the band toward the back. A line through the two hubs is nearly level, but the cylinder's cross-sections (shown by the band) run steeply down to the right. So the hubs aren't opposite ends of one axis at right angles to the lamp body, and the yoke reads as flat to the picture while the lamp is turned three-quarter.

m05_1.what: The body is clearly turned away from the viewer, with thick side walls showing at the bottom and right and the face leaning back toward the upper left. Yet the keys are drawn front-on as equal, nearly square caps. The far keys (7, 8, 9, ÷) are hardly smaller or flatter than the near ones (0, ., =, +). No key shows its bottom or right side wall the way the body does. The keypad reads as a flat front-view sticker pasted onto a tilted object.

The rows slope with the body's top edge, but the gaps and key widths stay even across the whole face instead of tightening toward the far upper-left corner. The bottom row also tilts a little more steeply than the top row, so the rows do not converge in a steady way toward one vanishing point.

m05_2.what: The body is tilted back and turned, so its face recedes toward the top. Yet every key is drawn almost front-on at the same size and spacing: the far 7-8-9-÷ row is as large and wide as the near 0-.-=-+ row. The keys do not shrink or flatten with the face, and their visible side walls all face the same way. The key grid reads as a flat sticker laid over the tilted body, not as keys set into its surface. This is the same mistake as in the first reference example.

The key rows slope down to the right more steeply than the top edge of the body and the bottom edge of the display. The key columns also lean differently from the left and right sides of the body. So the grid does not sit on lines parallel to the face's edges, and the keypad looks rotated against the body.

m16_1.what: The frame does not add up. The left X runs along the side of the chair, but the second X spans the front, from the front-left seat corner to the far-right foot. The front-left corner has two tubes running down to different feet. A real folding chair has two matching side X's linked by cross rails, so this frame could not fold, and its four feet do not form a proper rectangle.

The right back post ends at the seat with no leg or X under it. The left post continues down into a leg, so the two sides do not match, and the rear-right of the seat and backrest has nothing underneath to hold it.

The seat and legs are turned well into three-quarter view: the seat's front and back edges climb steeply to the right. The backrest is drawn almost flat to the camera. Its top edge is nearly horizontal and both of its ends are about the same height. It reads as a front view laid onto a chair that is turned to the side, so the backrest does not share the seat's rear edge direction.

The near front edge of the seat, between the two front joints, comes out slightly shorter than the far back edge between the two back posts. Perspective should make the nearer edge equal or longer. This slight reverse perspective makes the seat look a little wedge-shaped.

m17_1.what: The round clock stands upright on its curved rim with no stand, feet or back prop. A disc resting on a single point could not stay upright and would roll or fall over.

m17_2.what: The clock stands upright on its rounded rim with no feet, stand or flat base. A round desk clock balanced on its curved edge would roll or tip over. Real standing clocks have small feet or a flattened base. The shadow reads as resting on the floor, so this is a missing support part and not floating.

m35_2.what: The tabletop is seen from high above: a deep top face with the whole board laid out. The pedestal and plinth under it are seen almost level and front-on: flat front faces, the plinth's top barely visible, and no side planes receding with the top's edges. The upper and lower halves of the table read as two different camera heights.

The board does not follow the tabletop's edges. Its left edge runs at a clearly different angle from the tabletop's left edge, so the border is wide at the front-left and thin at the back-right. The squares stay nearly the same size from front to back instead of shrinking and bunching toward the far edge. The grid looks pasted on and slightly rotated rather than lying in the table's plane.

The stool tops are fairly open ellipses, but the base rings below them are drawn almost flat. Because the bases sit further below eye level, their ellipses should be at least as open as the tops, or more.

m36_1.what: The pier leads nowhere. The deck's front edge is raised over the water and stops at the front posts. It never reaches the sand, and no step or ramp comes down to the beach. Nobody could walk onto it from shore, which is a pier's whole job.
The rope is three closed rings with no free end and no tie-off. It is not a wound rope that starts or ends anywhere, and nothing ties it to the pier or to a boat.

The two front posts hold up the same front beam, so they are the same distance from the camera. Even so, the right post meets the water noticeably lower than the left one, and it is also a little wider and taller. That puts one post closer to the viewer than the other, which does not fit the squarely front-facing beam between them.

The far-end posts are drawn only slightly smaller than the front posts. Compared with how much the deck narrows (about 0.4 of its front width), they should be smaller still. Their top ellipses are also nearly as open as the front posts' tops, even though they sit just under the horizon and should be flatter.

m36_2.what: The rope has no ends. It forms two closed rings that merge into each other around the post, with no tail and no knot. A real wrapped rope has to start and finish somewhere, for example a tail hanging down or tied off, or a knot. This is a smaller version of the rope fault in the reference pier.

m04_1.what: The truss is a short, finished piece with capped tube ends on both sides inside the frame. It does not run out of the picture and is not hung or mounted on anything, so the beam and the light float in mid-air.

The back upper and lower tubes only show past the right end of the front pair, and nothing braces them to the front tubes. The diagonals only make sense for the front face, so the truss is not clearly a solid box or a flat ladder truss.

The yoke lies flat in the picture plane, and its pivot knob shows the tilt axis runs straight left to right. A lamp held that way can only tilt up and down, so the body's axis should look vertical on screen, pointing straight down or toward the viewer. Instead the body swings strongly to the lower left, which needs the yoke to be turned too. The yoke and the body are drawn from two different viewpoints.

The yoke has no depth, yet the body fills it edge to edge and its back end bulges past the right arm. The body looks pasted over the bracket rather than held between two arms that sit on either side of it in depth.
The lenses are drawn as roughly level, near-circular ovals. They do not follow the tilt and squash of the rim ellipse around them, so they face the camera more directly than the face they sit on.

m04_2.what: Diagonals don't form a regular zigzag: some cross mid-span, the ends don't meet the chords at matching joints, and the front and back faces don't line up
Left arm ends against the top of the can with no pivot knob to match the right side, and its length doesn't quite match the right arm

The yoke faces the camera straight on, so the axis between its two arms runs flat across the picture. A lamp turning on that axis can only tilt toward or away from the viewer. This lamp instead swings diagonally toward the lower left. The two arms also end at different heights: the left arm stops on top of the can with no pivot, and the right arm drops to a knob at mid-body. The holder and the lamp are seen from two different angles, and the lamp is not mounted on the axis the yoke shows.

The back tubes stick out past the front tubes at the right end, offset sideways only. No diagonals or cross-ties are shown in the back or side faces. So the truss reads as a flat front ladder with longer tubes behind it, not one solid box seen from a single viewpoint.

m05_1.what: The face's top and bottom edges get closer together toward the right, and the right edge is shorter than the left, so the right side recedes. The keys ignore this. The cyan keys on the far right are as wide and tall as the near-left navy keys, or slightly bigger, and the gaps between keys do not tighten toward the right. Size foreshortening across the face is missing, although the rows do roughly follow the face's tilt.

m16_1.what: The two sides are built differently. The right back upright carries straight down to the back-right foot as one leg, but the left upright ends at the seat. The back frame is attached to the base on one side only, so the chair could neither hold together nor fold the same way on both sides.
There is no rear seat tube. The back edge of the canvas and the tops of the rear X legs have nothing to fix to. The seat hangs from the front tube alone and could not hold a sitter's weight.
The front tube runs past the leg joint on the left side and ends in mid-air, with no leg or joint holding that end.

The backrest does not sit on the seat's back edge at the same width and angle. The right upright lands on the seat's back-right corner. The left upright lands well inside the seat's back-left corner, partway along the back edge. The backrest looks narrower than the seat and turned more toward the viewer than the seat and legs, as if the two were drawn from slightly different angles.

The two uprights are not parallel. The left one is vertical. The right one leans out to the right toward the top and lines up with the slanted X-leg below it, so the backrest flares and looks twisted instead of being a flat rectangle standing upright.

m16_2.what: The left back post stops at the seat. The tube from the front-left foot stops at the pivot. The piece of tube that should join them below the seat is missing, so the left back post is not tied to the legs, unlike the right side, where the back post runs down through the pivot to the foot. As drawn, the left side of the back has no support below the seat.

The front of the seat hangs from a tube, but no matching tube or bar runs across the back. The back edge of the seat fabric is stretched between the posts with nothing holding it, so it could not carry a sitter's weight.

m35_1.what: The stool seats are drawn as fairly round ellipses, about 0.4 as tall as they are wide, as if seen from well above. The table's top surface and its base slab are much flatter, about 0.2–0.25, as if seen from closer to level. The base slab lies on the ground, below the seats, so with one camera its top should look at least as open as the seats, not flatter. As drawn, the stool tops look tipped toward the viewer compared with the table.

m35_2.what: The table top is squashed far more than the stools. The square slab's top face is only about 15–18% as deep as it is wide, as if seen from almost eye level, but the stool seats beside it are about 45% as deep as they are wide, seen clearly from above. The table is a little higher, which allows a slightly flatter view, but not a difference this big. The table top looks tipped up toward the viewer and doesn't share one camera with the stools and the ground.

The board squares are drawn as wide, flat bars in uneven rows. The board shows clearly more columns than rows (it looks like about 10 across and 6 deep) instead of an 8×8 grid foreshortened evenly toward the back edge, so the grid doesn't follow a square surface.

The plinth's top face is also very thin (about 30 px deep for 240 px wide) for something so close to the ground, where the high camera should show it fairly open, like the stool seats. It has the same too-low view as the table top.

m36_1.what: These piles all hang from the same straight front edge, so they should look about the same length and their bases should sit on one water line. Instead they get steadily longer from left to right, by roughly 75 → 110 → 135 → 155 px in the enlarged view. Their bases also drop toward the viewer about twice as fast as the deck edge above them. The water surface and the deck therefore don't agree on one ground plane, and the right end of the pier seems raised higher above the water than the left.

The ring is drawn as a full, slightly tall circle facing the camera straight on. Hanging upright on the pier's front face and seen from above, it should look a little squashed from top to bottom. It should also turn slightly with the front face, which recedes to the right. As drawn, it looks pasted flat onto the picture rather than lying in the pier's space.

m36_2.what: The waterlines of the front posts drop much faster to the right than the deck's front beam does. In the enlarged view, the deck edge falls only about 50 px from the second front post to the right corner, but the post bottoms fall about 80 px. The posts therefore get visibly longer below the deck toward the right, as if the flat water tilted or the right corner stood closer to the camera than the deck edge shows. The bases should sit on a line parallel to the deck edge.

The ring hangs on a vertical face but is drawn as a full circle, even slightly taller than wide. The camera looks down about 30°, as the post-top ellipses and the deck show, so a ring hanging upright should look slightly squashed top-to-bottom (a wide ellipse).

render_m04.what: The red emitter runs past the bezel rim at the lower right, and the yellow one sits on the rim at the upper left. The emitters are not inside the lens opening, so they look stuck on the outside of the housing.

The three beams are drawn as solid, overlapping glass-like cones that pass through each other. There are crumpled shapes inside them, and each cone ends in a hard, capped edge, like a physical object instead of light that fades out. Their edges also fan out in different directions instead of forming one beam along the can's axis.
The left arm runs down into the top of the can and stops there, with no pivot knob to match the one on the right. The yoke holds the can on one side only, and the left arm is a loose end.

The yellow, white and red lenses are drawn as flat, wide ellipses tilted their own way, while the rim around them is an almost round ellipse. Lenses that sit flush in that face should be ellipses with the rim's narrowness and tilt, so they look flatter and turned differently from the face they are set in.

render_m16.what: The two sides of the frame are not mirror images. The right backrest upright bends at seat level and carries on down as one leg of the right X to the front-right foot. The left upright stops at the seat, and the left X is a separate pair of legs that never joins the backrest. One side cannot be built like the other, and the backrest is only held up on one side.
The rear leg of the left X ends under the middle of the seat canvas, where there is no seat rail or joint to hold it. The leg attaches to nothing and could not carry the seat.

The front rail sticks out well past the seat canvas on the left, and the canvas covers only part of it. The seat is skewed: the front rail and the backrest are offset sideways, so the seat is not a proper rectangle stretched between matching side rails.
A thin gap shows between the top edge of the backrest canvas and the top bar, so the canvas does not hang from the bar. Nothing clearly holds the panel at its top.

render_m36.what: The pile hangs from the deck and ends in a sharp point in mid-air in front of the sand bank. It does not reach the sand or the water, so it supports nothing. The deck's shore end just hangs over the bank with no footing or ramp onto the sand, so the pier is not properly tied to the shore.

The ring hangs from a pile stub that rises out of the walkway, and its lower half passes into the front edge of the deck instead of hanging clear of it. A real lifebuoy hangs on the outside face of a post or railing, clear of the planks.
The 'rope' is three closed, separate rings stacked on the pile, with no running end and no tie-off. A rope wrapped around a post is one continuous strand with at least one end hanging or knotted.

This support ends in a sharp point hanging in the air at the bank's edge. It does not go down into the sand or the water, so the deck's land end has no clear contact with its ground. It reads as floating over the sloped bank instead of resting on it.
